P.n: Nintendo Museum (ニンテンドーミュージアム)
P.w: Nintendo's own museum, opened 2 Oct 2024 in the former Uji Ogura plant where it made hanafuda cards and repaired consoles — 135 years from playing cards to Switch, with hands-on exhibits.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Nintendo (Mario, Zelda, Pokémon) — the company's only museum, in its Kyoto home turf.

P.w: Nintendo's 1930s original head office (used until 1959), the 'Yamauchi Nintendo' plaques still on the façade, reopened April 2022 as a Tadao Ando-designed hotel; the exterior is viewable from the street.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Nintendo — the building where the playing-card firm Marufuku/Yamauchi Nintendo was run before video games.

P.n: Demachi Masugata Shōtengai (出町桝形商店街)
P.ad: Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto (Demachi, just west of the Kamo River delta)
P.w: A 164 m retro local arcade at the end of the old Saba Kaidō mackerel road, with the Demachi-za mini-theatre — the real model for the Usagiyama shopping street in Kyoto Animation's Tamako Market.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Tamako Market (Kyoto Animation, 2013) — model for Usagiyama Shōtengai; the arcade openly welcomes fans.

P.w: 'Kyoto's Kitchen' — a narrow five-block covered street of more than a hundred food shops (the first opened around 1310): pickles, fresh yuba, dashi-maki tamago, seasonal Kyoto produce and knives.
Lantern-lit lane of teahouses and restaurants squeezed between the Kamo River and Kiyamachi — one of Kyoto's five geisha districts, with summer kawayuka dining platforms over the river.
Head temple of the Ōtani branch of Jōdo Shinshū near Kyoto Station; its Goeidō founder's hall is Kyoto's largest wooden structure. Free to enter.
Hiroshi Hara's 1997 glass-and-steel station building, built for the city's 1,200th anniversary — the giant atrium staircase climbs to a free rooftop skyway with city views.
The 131-metre tower opposite Kyoto Station, the city's tallest structure; the observation deck at 100 m gives a 360° view to Osaka on clear days.
JR West's museum (2016) by Umekōji Park with more than 50 retired trains, from steam locomotives in a working roundhouse to shinkansen; closed Wednesdays.
Japan's first manga museum, in a 1929 elementary-school building by Karasuma-Oike Station, with some 300,000 items and walls of manga you can pull down and read.
Small shrine to Sugawara no Michizane at the east end of Nishiki Market, wedged into the Shinkyōgoku shopping arcade — its torii's ends literally run into the neighbouring buildings.
City history-and-culture museum on Sanjō-dōri, partly housed in the 1906 red-brick former Bank of Japan Kyoto branch; regular film screenings.
Hexagonal temple said to be founded by Prince Shōtoku, birthplace of ikebana — the Ikenobō school's headquarters and Ikebana Museum stand in its grounds.
Modern inland aquarium (2012) in Umekōji Park, a 15-minute walk west of Kyoto Station, with a Kyoto-rivers zone of Japanese giant salamanders.
Temple founded in 991 for Jizō, guardian of children, and HQ ground of the Shinsengumi — graves of commander Kondō Isami and members lie in its Mibu-zuka; famous for its Kyōgen mime plays.
Higashi Hongan-ji's 17th-century detached garden ('Kikoku-tei'), a nationally designated Place of Scenic Beauty a short walk from Kyoto Station.
Former inn for visiting daimyō, riddled with secret passages, trap doors and hidden escape routes; guided tours by reservation.
Kyoto's oldest licensed pleasure quarter (1641): pass the Ōmon gate to Edo-period Wachigaiya and Sumiya, one of the city's largest machiya, now a seasonally opening museum of hospitality culture.
Two parallel covered shopping streets branching north off Shijō at Kawaramachi, packed with shops, temples and cheap eats — a younger crowd than Shijō's department stores.
Remnant of the imperial palace garden laid out with Heian-kyō in 794 — the 'Garden of the Holy Spring', a pond and island just south of Nijō Castle.
Temple rebuilt on Teramachi after the 1582 Honnō-ji Incident, in which Oda Nobunaga died at its original site; his memorial tower stands here.
Head shrine of the thousands of Inari shrines across Japan, dedicated to the god of rice and sake by the Hata clan in the 8th century — tunnels of thousands of vermilion torii climb Mount Inari.
Museum of Gekkeikan, one of Fushimi's largest and oldest brewers, in a renovated 1909 sake storehouse beside the Horikawa canal — traditional brewing tools and a tasting at the end.
Site of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's retirement castle on Momoyama hill, around which the Fushimi sake town grew; today's keep is a modern reconstruction.
The Fushimi boat-inn where Sakamoto Ryōma was attacked by shogunate police in 1866; rebuilt after the 1868 Battle of Toba–Fushimi and open to visitors with Bakumatsu relics.
Willow-lined Horikawa canal quarter of storehouses and some 20–40 breweries drawing on Fushimi's soft spring water — one of Japan's great sake towns; tastings and canal boat rides.
Replica Edo-period covered riverboats glide 50 minutes down the Horikawa canal past the wood-and-plaster walls of Fushimi's sake breweries (seasonal).
Shingon temple in Ono (Yamashina) on the site of the Heian poet Ono no Komachi's residence — prayed at for romantic matches; its plum garden blooms in March.
Head temple of the Shingon Yamashina school, an imperial-linked temple with a broad Heian-style pond garden.
Hino's Fujiwara-era temple whose Amida Hall and seated Amida statue are National Treasures.
Shrine founded with the Heian capital in 794 to guard its south; famed for its gardens tracing Japanese garden history and its weeping plums.
Emperor Meiji's tumulus on the old Fushimi Castle hill, reached by a long, wide stone stairway through the woods.
Ōbaku temple just south of Fushimi Inari whose hillside holds hundreds of stone rakan designed by the painter Itō Jakuchū.
Fukakusa shrine near Keihan Fujinomori Station, associated with horses and victory and known for its hydrangea garden.
Eastern Kyoto's hillside temple, famous for the wooden terrace with a view over the city; part of the UNESCO 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto'.
One of Kyoto's best-preserved historic districts — narrow lanes, wooden buildings and merchant shops on the 20–30 minute walk from Kiyomizu-dera to Yasaka Shrine.
Gion's great shrine, home of the Gion Matsuri every July for over a thousand years; busiest at cherry-blossom time beside Maruyama Park.
Public park next to Yasaka Shrine; in early April Kyoto's most popular (and most crowded) hanami spot under the weeping cherry.
Kyoto's most famous geisha district, between Yasaka Shrine and the Kamo River — ochaya teahouses where geiko and maiko entertain.
Founded 1606 by Nene in memory of Toyotomi Hideyoshi; a tsukiyama pond garden of man-made hills, pine and maple. Its sub-temple Entoku-in adds two more Zen gardens.
Head temple of the Jōdo (Pure Land) sect; its Sanmon, 24 m tall and 50 m wide, is the largest wooden temple gate in Japan (early 1600s).
Tendai monzeki temple whose head priests were traditionally imperial; houses the National Treasure painting of the Blue Cetaka (Ao Fudō) and a garden attributed to Sōami.

P.ad: Komatsu-chō (south of Gion), Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto, Japan
P.w: Founded 1202 — the oldest Zen temple in Kyoto, ranked third of the city's five great Zen temples, just south of Gion.
The five-storey Yasaka Pagoda rising over the Higashiyama lanes on the walk up to Kiyomizu-dera.
One of the Kyoto Gozan (five great Zen temples), founded in the 13th century; its Tsūten-kyō bridge over a maple valley is one of Kyoto's most famous autumn-leaf views.
Founded in 951 by the itinerant monk Kūya — the 17th temple of the Saigoku Kannon pilgrimage — in Rokuhara, the old Heike warrior quarter; its Kūya statue shows tiny Buddhas issuing from his mouth.
One of Japan's four national museums, in the Higashiyama temple district opposite Sanjūsangen-dō; Kyoto's major collection of pre-modern Japanese and Asian art.
The 120-metre hall of 1266 (National Treasure) housing 1,001 standing Thousand-armed Kannon statues, flanked by Fūjin and Raijin.

Head temple of the Chisan school of Shingon Buddhism, opposite the Kyoto National Museum; known for its early-Edo pond garden and Momoyama-period Hasegawa school screen paintings that are National Treasures.
Imperial family temple ('Mitera') whose origin traces to the 820s–830s, with imperial mausolea in its wooded precinct below Tōfuku-ji; head of the Sennyū-ji branch of Shingon.
The 'Ear Mound' — a sobering burial mound for the ears and noses taken as trophies from Korean and Chinese soldiers in Hideyoshi's 1590s invasions of Korea; a national Historic Site.
Shrine for cutting bad ties and binding good ones: crawl through the hole in the paper-covered 'enkiri-enmusubi' stone to make your wish.
Temple at the old 'crossroads of the six realms' by the Toribeno burial ground; its well is said to be where the courtier Ono no Takamura descended nightly to the underworld.
Kōdai-ji sub-temple built after 1605 by Nene, Hideyoshi's widow, where she spent her last years — two rock gardens and painted screens.
Shrine to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, prayed at for career success; its karamon gate with carved carp and cranes is a National Treasure. Next to Hōkō-ji's great bell.
Walled Rinzai Zen complex of some two dozen sub-temples — one of the best places in Japan to see a range of Zen gardens and tea culture.
Head of the shrines to the scholar Sugawara no Michizane — students pray here before exams; famous for its plum grove and its monthly flea market on the 25th.
Daitoku-ji sub-temple famed for its maple-lined bamboo approach and moss garden — one of Kyoto's best autumn-colour spots.
Kyoto's oldest geiko district, by Kitano Tenmangū in the Nishijin weaving quarter; its geiko and maiko serve at the shrine's Baikasai plum tea ceremony every 25 February.
Shrine north of Daitoku-ji prayed to for a fortunate marriage ('tama-no-koshi'); at its east gate two rival shops have grilled aburi-mochi rice cakes for centuries.
Shrine to Abe no Seimei, the Heian court diviner (onmyōji), marked by star-pentagram crests; a pilgrimage spot for fans of onmyōji fiction.
Ancient shrine near Kitano Tenmangū, long one of Kyoto's classic cherry-blossom (hanami) spots.
Retired Emperor Go-Mizunoo's 1630 palace in Kyoto Gyoen; free guided tours through its North and South Pond stroll gardens.
Takagamine Zen temple famous for its two windows on the garden — the square 'Window of Confusion' and round 'Window of Enlightenment' — and a 'blood ceiling' of floorboards from Fushimi Castle.
Quiet temple in the northern hills whose dry garden of clipped azaleas borrows distant Mount Hiei as scenery; another Fushimi Castle 'blood ceiling'.
Nichiren temple on land Tokugawa Ieyasu granted the artist Hon'ami Kōetsu for his arts colony in Takagamine; known for its bamboo 'Kōetsu fence' and maples.
Shingon temple founded in 1221 whose Main Hall (Shakadō) is the oldest standing Buddhist hall in Kyoto — a National Treasure that survived the Ōnin War.
Head temple of the Shōkoku-ji school of Rinzai Zen just north of the Imperial Palace — parent temple of both Kinkaku-ji and Ginkaku-ji.
Tendai temple on the site of Murasaki Shikibu's residence, east of the Imperial Palace, with a raked-gravel and moss 'Genji garden' of bellflowers.
The 3 km pine-covered sandbar across Miyazu Bay, one of the 'Three Views of Japan' — viewed upside-down through your legs (matanozoki) from the hilltop parks at either end.
Fishing village of funaya — wooden boathouses with living quarters above, built right over the water around Ine Bay; best seen from a bay cruise.
Shingon temple on wollastonite rocks above the Seta River, where Murasaki Shikibu is said to have begun The Tale of Genji; its main hall and Tahōtō pagoda are National Treasures.
Head temple of the Tendai Jimon school at the foot of Mount Hiei above Lake Biwa; its Kondō is a National Treasure and its evening bell one of the Eight Views of Ōmi.
Head shrine of the Hie/Hiyoshi shrines, guardian of Enryaku-ji in the Sakamoto foothills of Mount Hiei; its East and West main halls are National Treasures and the grounds famous for autumn maples.
Saigoku pilgrimage temple in the hills on the north side of Amanohashidate, with a celebrated lookout over the sandbar.
Ancient shrine at the north end of Amanohashidate, called 'Moto-Ise' for its link to the Grand Shrine of Ise.
Heian-period Pure Land temple in rural southern Kyoto Prefecture: nine Amida statues in a long hall facing a three-storey pagoda across a pond — both National Treasures.
Mountain temple in Kamo, Kizugawa, whose small Kamakura-period five-storey pagoda is a National Treasure.
Hillside park above Kono Shrine, reached by chairlift or cable car, from where Amanohashidate is said to look like the kanji for 'one' — the classic upside-down matanozoki viewpoint.
Descent of the Hozu Gorge from Kameoka to Arashiyama in flat-bottomed boats steered by boatmen with oars and bamboo poles — often paired with the Sagano Scenic Railway.
Ōhara's great Tendai temple, its origins traced to the monk Saichō: moss gardens with small jizō statues under maples, at its finest in mid-November.
Small Ōhara temple near Sanzen-in, viewed 'like a picture frame' from the tatami room with matcha — its centrepiece is a carefully pruned 700-year-old pine.
Mountain temple on Mount Kurama, legendary training ground of the young warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsune; a forest trail crosses the ridge down to Kibune.
Shrine to the god of water up the Kibune valley, its stone steps lined with red lanterns; summer visitors dine on kawadoko platforms over the river below.
Shingon temple founded in 781, up a few hundred stone steps in the Takao maple valley — one of Kyoto's three classic autumn-leaf gorges; throw clay kawarake discs off the cliff for luck.
Ōhara nunnery founded around 600, where Empress Kenreimon-in retired after the fall of the Heike — a closing scene of The Tale of the Heike.
Small Shingon temple in Makinoo between Jingo-ji and Kōzan-ji, one of the 'three o' maple gorges of Takao.
Yase villa-temple open only in seasonal windows, famous for maples reflected in its polished black lacquer desk ('yuka-momiji').
Mountain village of nearly 40 thatched-roof farmhouses — the highest proportion of thatched houses anywhere in Japan; a preserved historic district.
The most accessible hot spring from Kyoto, with indoor and outdoor baths at the upper end of Kurama village; it reopened in November 2024 after closing during the pandemic.
Arashiyama's 'Moon-Crossing Bridge' over the Katsura River — a landmark since the Heian period, last rebuilt in the 1930s, framed by the forested Arashiyama hills.
The roughly 400-metre path through towering bamboo between Tenryū-ji's north gate and Nonomiya Shrine — go at dawn to beat the crowds.
Silent-film star Ōkōchi Denjirō's hillside villa at the top of the bamboo grove — gardens, teahouses and a matcha with views over Kyoto.
Sagano temple holding some 8,000 stone Buddhas and statues for the souls of the dead, with its own small bamboo grove; candle-lit Sentō Kuyō in August.
A ten-minute hike up from just south of Togetsukyō to a hilltop where dozens of Japanese macaques roam freely, with a view over Kyoto.
At the far end of Sagano, a temple of 1,200 moss-softened stone rakan statues, each carved by a different amateur sculptor with its own expression.
Emperor Saga's 9th-century detached palace turned Shingon temple, beside the Ōsawa Pond — one of Japan's oldest surviving garden ponds and a moon-viewing spot.
Small shrine in the bamboo grove with a rare black (unbarked) torii, where imperial princesses purified themselves before serving at Ise; appears in The Tale of Genji.
One of Kyoto's oldest shrines (701), patron of sake brewers — barrels donated by breweries line the grounds — with Shigemori Mirei's Shōwa-era gardens.
Founded in 603 by the Hata clan — Kyoto's oldest temple — whose Reihōden treasure hall holds the serene Miroku Bosatsu, Japan's first National Treasure sculpture.
Uzumasa film-set theme park — Edo-period streets still used to shoot samurai dramas, with ninja shows and costume photo studios.
Walled Rinzai Zen complex of about 50 sub-temples, head of a school of over 3,000 temples, founded in 1337 when a retired emperor gave his villa to Zen.
Hillside temple on Mount Ogura above the bamboo grove — quiet most of the year, spectacular when its maples turn in autumn.
Sagano temple named for its two Buddha statues, Shaka and Amida, approached up a long maple-lined avenue.
Tiny thatched nunnery in a luxuriant moss garden, named for the dancer Giō who retreated here after Taira no Kiyomori spurned her.
'Saga Shakadō', famed for its wooden Buddha statue and as a training centre of Yūzū nembutsu.
Two-kilometre canal-side stone path from Ginkaku-ji to the Nanzen-ji neighbourhood, named for philosopher Nishida Kitarō's daily meditative walk; lined with cherry trees.

Head temple of the Nanzen-ji school of Rinzai Zen at the foot of the Higashiyama hills — the massive Sanmon gate, Hōjō rock garden and the brick Meiji-era Lake Biwa Canal aqueduct running through the grounds.
Jōdo temple north of Nanzen-ji, among Kyoto's most famous autumn-colour spots with evening illuminations in November; known for its 'looking-back' Amida statue.
Shrine built in 1895 for the 1,100th anniversary of the capital, its giant vermilion torii towering over Okazaki; the stroll garden behind is one of Kyoto's best for weeping cherry trees.
Quiet temple just off the Philosopher's Path with a moss-thatched gate and raked sand mounds — the most notable temple on the walk, especially in autumn.

P.n: Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art
P.w: Opened in 1933 as the Enthronement Memorial Museum — Japan's oldest public art museum still in its original building, renovated by Jun Aoki; Okazaki Park.

P.n: National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto
P.w: Fumihiko Maki-designed national museum facing the KYOCERA across the Heian Jingū approach, strong on Kyoto-school painting and modern ceramics (Kawai Kanjirō).
Statesman Yamagata Aritomo's 1894 villa with a lawn-and-stream garden by Ogawa Jihei borrowing the Higashiyama hills; a nationally designated Place of Scenic Beauty.
Nanzen-ji sub-temple whose crane-and-turtle garden by Kobori Enshū is a Special Place of Scenic Beauty.

Retired Emperor Go-Mizunoo's 1655 hillside villa of three gardens stepped among rice terraces at the foot of Mount Hiei; free Imperial Household Agency tours by reservation; Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
Daitoku-ji sub-temple with one of Japan's finest small dry landscape gardens — a 'river' of white gravel flowing from rock 'mountains'; Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
The 17th-century princely villa often called the pinnacle of Japanese garden and architectural design — teahouses around a stroll-garden pond; Imperial Household Agency tours by reservation.
The emperors' residence until 1868, inside the vast Kyoto Gyoen park; the palace grounds are free to visit without reservation.
The 'Hall of Immortal Poets', a scholar-poet's 1641 mountain hermitage hung with portraits of 36 Chinese poets, looking onto a white-sand garden of clipped azaleas and maples.
Tendai monzeki temple near Shugakuin, 'almost a temple within a garden': a sea of raked white gravel with islands of trees, rock and moss.
Tendai temple founded in 984 on the Yoshida hills, its pagoda and maples one of Kyoto's quieter famous autumn-leaf spots.
Large public botanical garden in Kitayama by the Kamo River, with a big conservatory and seasonal flower collections.
Disused inclined railway of the Meiji-era Lake Biwa Canal that hauled boats until the 1950s; the tracks are now a walk under about a hundred cherry trees.
Uji's 'flower temple' in the northern hills, founded some 1,200 years ago — vast gardens of azaleas, hydrangeas and lotuses in season.
Head temple of the Ōbaku school of Zen, founded by the Chinese monk Ingen in 1661 in Ming-dynasty Chinese style — and the home of fucha ryōri, Chinese-style vegetarian temple cuisine.
The large park at the heart of old Nara holding Tōdai-ji, Kasuga Taisha, Kōfuku-ji and the National Museum, roamed by more than a thousand free-ranging, bowing sika deer.
National museum of Japanese Buddhist art in Nara Park; its autumn Shōsō-in exhibition of 8th-century imperial treasures is a national event.
Two-part stroll garden (mid-17th century front, 1899 rear) that borrows Tōdai-ji's Nandaimon gate and Mount Wakakusa as scenery.
The grass-covered hill behind Nara Park between Tōdai-ji and Kasuga Taisha, with open views over the city; its slopes are set alight each January in the Yamayaki.
Nara-period temple founded by an empress praying for the ailing emperor; the main hall rings the Yakushi Buddha with twelve clay guardian generals.
Tōdai-ji's hillside hall with a free veranda view over Nara; stage of the Shuni-e (Omizutori) fire rite each March, held every year without a break for over 1,270 years.
Founded in 607 by Prince Shōtoku; its pagoda and Golden Hall are the world's oldest surviving wooden buildings — Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site (Buddhist Monuments in the Hōryū-ji Area).
Sōtō Zen temple across the Uji River from Byōdō-in, approached up the maple-lined 'Kotozaka' slope.
Uji city museum on The Tale of Genji, whose final 'Uji chapters' are set here — models, costumes and a film, with some English displays.
The main bridge over the Uji River, first built around 646 — one of Japan's oldest bridge sites — with Tsuen tea house at its east end.
Nara garden of moss, pond and tea-ceremony sections beside Isui-en, on the site of a Kōfuku-ji sub-temple.
Nara's former merchant quarter near Kintetsu Nara Station — narrow lanes of preserved and restored machiya townhouses, cafés and small museums.
One of Kyoto's oldest Shinto shrines, older than the city itself, with its two sand cones (tatesuna) before the Hosodono hall; UNESCO-listed component 688-001.
Ancient shrine at the meeting of the Kamo and Takano rivers, reached through the Tadasu-no-Mori primeval forest; UNESCO-listed component 688-002.

Founded in 796 as the guardian temple at the old capital's south gate; its five-storey pagoda is Japan's tallest wooden pagoda, and a flea market fills the grounds on the 21st of each month. UNESCO 688-003.
Head temple of Tendai Buddhism, founded on Mount Hiei in 788 and spread across the forested summit above Lake Biwa; UNESCO 688-005 (coordinate is the property centre of a 498 ha precinct).
Vast Shingon temple complex whose five-storey pagoda (951) is the oldest building in Kyoto; Toyotomi Hideyoshi's famous cherry-blossom party was held here. UNESCO 688-006.
Former imperial temple (founded 888) known for its late-blooming Omuro dwarf cherry trees and five-storey pagoda; UNESCO 688-007.
The 11th-century Phoenix Hall pictured on the 10-yen coin, reflected in its Pure Land garden pond; UNESCO 688-008.
Small shrine across the Uji River from Byōdō-in whose main hall is regarded as Japan's oldest surviving shrine building; UNESCO 688-009.
Mountain temple in Toganoo above Takao, keeper of the Chōjū-giga animal scrolls often called Japan's first manga; UNESCO 688-010.
The 'Moss Temple' — a garden carpeted with over a hundred kinds of moss; visits are by advance reservation only. UNESCO 688-011.
Head temple of the Rinzai Tenryū-ji school, founded 1339, with Musō Soseki's Sōgen pond garden borrowing the Arashiyama hills; UNESCO 688-012.
The Golden Pavilion — a gold-leafed Zen reliquary hall over a mirror pond, rebuilt in 1955 after arson; UNESCO 688-013.
The Silver Pavilion, Ashikaga Yoshimasa's retirement villa turned Zen temple, with its raked-sand garden and moss paths at the head of the Philosopher's Path; UNESCO 688-014.
Home of Japan's most famous dry rock garden — fifteen stones on raked gravel; UNESCO 688-015.
Head temple of the Jōdo Shinshū Hongwanji-ha, a short walk from Kyoto Station, with vast Founder's and Amida halls and Momoyama-era gates; UNESCO 688-016.
The Tokugawa shoguns' Kyoto residence (1603), whose Ninomaru Palace 'nightingale floors' chirp underfoot; UNESCO 688-017.
Nara's great temple, whose Daibutsuden houses the 15-metre bronze Great Buddha; UNESCO 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara' 870-001.
Fujiwara clan temple whose five-storey pagoda rises over Nara Park, with a National Treasure Hall of Buddhist sculpture including the Ashura statue; UNESCO 870-002.
Vermilion shrine of the Fujiwara famed for its thousands of stone and bronze lanterns, set against the protected Kasugayama Primeval Forest; UNESCO 870-003.
Successor to Asuka-dera, Japan's first full-scale Buddhist temple; some roof tiles date to the 6th century. In the Naramachi old town. UNESCO 870-004.
Seventh-century imperial temple in western Nara whose East Pagoda is one of Japan's oldest; UNESCO 870-005.
Founded in 759 by the Chinese monk Ganjin (Jianzhen); its Golden Hall is the finest surviving Nara-period main hall. UNESCO 870-006.
The excavated site of the 8th-century imperial palace of Heijō-kyō, with the reconstructed Daigokuden and Suzakumon gate; UNESCO 870-007 (coordinate = centre of a 129 ha site).

F.w: Michelin Bib Gourmand udon house that began delivering meals to Gion teahouses and playhouses; queues form before opening for the onion udon heaped with Kyoto's Kujō spring onion.
The Takabashi ramen institution founded in 1947, five minutes' walk from Kyoto Station — the benchmark for Kyoto's soy-pork-bone style.
New Bib Gourmand 2026 — the chef mills his own buckwheat for 100% soba, near Daitoku-ji.
One MICHELIN Star — innovative hearth cooking off Sanjō near Shirakawa, Kyoto-farm vegetables at the centre.
One MICHELIN Star (2026; an inspectors' favourite dish) — French in Kamigyō, with ~30 Takagamine vegetables and charcoal-grilled meat.
Bib Gourmand oden counter in Gion; the long-simmered eggs and daikon are the draw.
Bib Gourmand by the Shirakawa canal — Kyoto home cooking built around donabe rice.
Bib Gourmand izakaya near Karasuma-Oike, famous for its iced sashimi bowl.
Bib Gourmand Japanese course in the Muromachi textile quarter — affordable Kyoto kappō.
One MICHELIN Star in Fushimi — chef Masashi Anpeiji's sauce-led light French cooking.

F.ad: 1F, Hotel The Mitsui Kyoto, 284 Nijo Aburanokojicho, Nakagyo-ku, Kyoto, 604-0051, Japan
F.w: MICHELIN-listed contemporary cuisine at Hotel The Mitsui by Nijō Castle, built on Fushimi's water and dashi.
MICHELIN-listed shōjin ryōri at the south gate of Myōshin-ji; soy-flour udon is the signature.
Two MICHELIN Stars (promoted 2026) — kyō-ryōri in the Muromachi quarter; the abalone appetiser is an inspectors' favourite.
New One MICHELIN Star 2026 — Korean royal court cuisine learned in Seoul, by Mibu-dera.
One MICHELIN Star — the deep-fried roe-ayu roll was a 2026 inspectors' favourite dish.
New One MICHELIN Star 2026 — a Nagasaki-accented Japanese counter in Shimogyō.
Added by MICHELIN inspectors July 2026 — a sake-led izakaya that opens with soup and tsukuri.
Added by MICHELIN inspectors July 2026 — a tempura counter in Saga-Arashiyama near Tenryū-ji.
One MICHELIN Star — a Gion tempura counter famed for its near-transparent coating.
MICHELIN-listed bistro by an Alsace-trained chef — the city's choucroute address.
Bib Gourmand (2026) unagi house in Uda, Nara — father-to-son Edo-style grilling learned in Tokyo.
MICHELIN-listed soba shop on a Naramachi sake brewery's premises, using the brewery's water.
One MICHELIN Star Chinese in Naramachi — a garden-to-wok vegetable-led course.
MICHELIN-listed Gion Chinese tailored to the geiko district — garlic- and lard-free.
MICHELIN-listed modern Chinese in Higashiyama — a tasting run of small plates.
New One MICHELIN Star 2026 (inspectors' reveal article) — fermentation-driven Japanese cooking in Kita-ku.
Added by MICHELIN inspectors July 2026 — a dashi-obsessed Kamigyō counter.
Added by MICHELIN inspectors July 2026 — ryōtei-trained chef cooking à la carte in an alley machiya.

One MICHELIN Star — Japanese technique with modern Italian flavour; the hamo-and-prosciutto is an inspectors' must-try.

Two MICHELIN Stars — in a century-old sukiya house near Kōdai-ji; the grilled wagyu is an inspectors' must-try.
Bib Gourmand pizzeria near Ginkaku-ji — the chef imported an Italian oven-builder for his oven.
MICHELIN-listed Shimogamo sushi house keeping the bite-size temari-zushi tradition alive.
MICHELIN-listed Nishijin restaurant where one chef makes both soba and sushi; the sesame tofu is renowned.
One MICHELIN Star — Alexis Moko (Paris/London-trained) cooking French in an old merchant's house with Kyoto produce.
MICHELIN-listed cross-cultural (French/Japanese/Chinese) cooking in a Nakagyō machiya; the Ōhara-vegetable salad is the calling card.
Bib Gourmand kushiage counter — inventive deep-fried skewers in extraordinary variety.
One MICHELIN Star (2026) — sister of Jiki Miyazawa; its signature yaki-gomadōfu heralds each season.
MICHELIN-listed (2026) Teramachi-Sanjō sukiyaki house (est. 1873), served table-side by nakai-san.
MICHELIN-listed (2026) tempura counter off Teramachi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand ramen shop in Ichijōji; the signature soy-sauce ramen uses a dashi of locally raised free-range chicken and water only, finished with a raw soy-sauce kaeshi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand noodle bar, relocated from Murasakino (Kita-ku) to Kamigyō-ku; house noodles of Kyoto wheat in a clear seafood-dashi broth seasoned with pure soy sauce.
Seven-generation eel house (Michelin Bib Gourmand); Kantō-style steamed-then-grilled kabayaki, famous for the kinshi-don.
Michelin Bib Gourmand soba restaurant in the Jōdo-ji quarter near Ginkaku-ji.
Michelin Bib Gourmand udon-and-soba house on the Heian Jingū approach in Okazaki, serving soft Kyoto-style udon in light dashi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand noodle shop in Gion serving udon and soba.

Michelin Bib Gourmand ramen shop west of Kyoto Station whose signature is a scallop and Japanese (sanshō) pepper ramen.
Michelin Bib Gourmand 'place of rice' run by a rice-loving owner, serving small plates built on seafood and citrus from his native Ehime.
Michelin Bib Gourmand specialising in locally raised chicken and obanzai; the house speciality is rare 'white liver'.
Michelin Bib Gourmand sake bar with rigorously chosen local sake; oden in a Rishiri-kombu broth and Seto Inland Sea octopus as chunks, oden or tempura.

Buddhist vegetarian temple cuisine served inside Tenryū-ji's World Heritage grounds (Michelin Bib Gourmand): sesame tofu, deep-fried tofu with vegetables, dressed greens.
Michelin-listed hand-cut soba shop in Murasakino, near Daitoku-ji.
Michelin-listed soba restaurant in central Nakagyō.
Michelin-listed soba restaurant in Shimogyō.
Michelin-listed soba house in Kamigyō named for its atsumori — warm soba served for dipping.

Three MICHELIN Stars (2026) kaiseki house in Maruyama Park.
Three MICHELIN Stars (2026) — a veteran ryōtei by Nanzen-ji whose rooms breathe wabi-sabi restraint.
Three MICHELIN Stars (2026); a house that began as a travelling fishmonger, now led by sixth-generation head Motokazu Nakamura.

New Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) on Fuyachō-dōri, built around seafood from Wakasa Bay and local Fukui sake.
New Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) ramen shop in Uzumasa, its bowls built on a chicken-and-pork broth.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2025) creative soba house; the famous 'Daigo Soba' is blanketed in Parmigiano Reggiano in imitation of daigo, an ancient Japanese cheese.
Ramen counter opened by a Nishijin kelp merchant (Michelin Bib Gourmand 2025): the soup uses no sauce at all, every drop of umami drawn from kombu.
Michelin Bib Gourmand in Yamashina, east of Fushimi, specialising in aged pork sourced from a Fushimi butcher.
Michelin Bib Gourmand soba restaurant in north-western Nara city.

Michelin Bib Gourmand kushiage counter in Nara: creative seasonal fried skewers with Nara touches (sake-lees pickles, goma-dōfu), ending in nyūmen or dashi chazuke made with rice grown by the chef's brother.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) Indian kitchen in Nara — 'toi' = 'trip of imagination' — serving meat, fish and vegetable curries thali-style as a teishoku.

One MICHELIN Star Chinese restaurant in Okazaki cooking with a seasonal Kyoto aesthetic.

Michelin Bib Gourmand Japanese restaurant run by a former fishmonger; seasonal menus whose hassun platters, garnished with flowers, recall traditional festival foods.
Michelin Bib Gourmand tempura-kaiseki house inherited from the chef's grandfather in Nishijin; its signature dresses tempura in chopped onion and mustard.
Michelin Bib Gourmand char-grill izakaya run by a former French chef — straw-smoked fish and venison and duck grilled as whole cuts.
Michelin Bib Gourmand sushi shop in Nakagyō delivering Kyoto-style sushi at a modest price.
Michelin Bib Gourmand Japanese kitchen whose inventive, patient cooking includes a salad dressed with heshiko mackerel.

Michelin Bib Gourmand yōshoku house keeping the previous generation's classics — gratin and cutlets — with French specials on the blackboard.
Michelin Bib Gourmand eel house founded at the end of the Edo period as a river-fish wholesaler; the fourth-generation chef's kinshi-don, under thin-cut omelette ribbons, is renowned.
Michelin Bib Gourmand casual offshoot of the three-star Kikunoi; its house speciality is shigure-meshi rice topped with sea bream sashimi in sesame sauce.
Michelin Bib Gourmand Cantonese kitchen — shrimp wontons, stir-fried squid with asparagus, seasonal soups.

F.ad: 140 Dōyū-chō, Sakaimachi-dōri Sanjō-sagaru, Nakagyō-ku, Kyoto 604-8118, Japan
F.w: Kyoto's classic kissaten, in business since 1940; the retro main shop serves a 'Kyoto breakfast' available only at the flagship.

F.ad: Beside Minami-za, Shijō-dōri, Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto, Japan
F.w: Founded in 1861 as a theatre teahouse; in 1882 the second-generation owner invented nishin soba and moved beside the Minami-za kabuki theatre — the dish has been a Kyoto speciality ever since.
Founded in 1465 and billed as Japan's oldest soba restaurant; stock made with Kyoto well water and freshly boiled buckwheat noodles.
Two MICHELIN Stars Japanese restaurant in Nara showcasing traditional cuisine shaped by the seasons.

F.n: Shinpuku Saikan Honten (新福菜館 本店)
F.ad: 569 Higashi-Shiokōji Mukaihata-chō, Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto (5 min walk from JR Kyoto Station)
F.w: The black-soup original of Kyoto ramen: a yatai from 1938, at this spot by Kyoto Station since 1944 — the dark broth tastes far lighter than it looks.

F.n: Chūka Soba Takayasu (中華そば 高安)
F.w: The originator of the cloudy, creamy-but-not-greasy broth that defines the Ichijōji ramen battleground; soup simmered 22+ hours.

F.n: François Kissashitsu (フランソア喫茶室)
F.ad: Nishikiyamachi-dōri by the Takase-gawa, Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto (1 min from Kyoto-Kawaramachi Stn)
F.w: Kyoto's iconic 1934 meikyoku-kissa; in 2003 the first café in Japan registered as a national Tangible Cultural Property.
Family-run since 1950 at Sanjō-Kawaramachi — two floors, two coffees; a cornerstone of Kyoto's kissaten culture.
Kyoto's third-wave pioneer, roasting its own beans since 2016, hidden in a machiya alley.

F.ad: Near JR Kyoto Station, Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto
F.w: Kyoto-born specialty brand that went global; a stand-up hand-drip bar a short walk from Kyoto Station.

F.ad: Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto (near Yasaka Pagoda and Kiyomizu-dera)
F.w: The minimalist % Arabica brand was born in Kyoto (2014); the Higashiyama shop is its flagship.

F.ad: Shijō-dōri, Gion, Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto (near Yasaka Shrine)
F.w: A Gion institution since the early 18th century; its tea room is the classic place for kuzukiri.

F.ad: Imamiya Shrine east approach, Murasakino, Kita-ku, Kyoto
F.w: The 'Honke' aburi-mochi house (c.1600), facing Ichiwa across Imamiya Shrine's approach.

F.n: Ichiwa (一和 / 一文字屋和輔)
F.ad: Imamiya Shrine east approach, Murasakino, Kita-ku, Kyoto
F.w: Said to be founded in 1000 (Chōhō 2) — among Japan's oldest confectioners; aburi-mochi at Imamiya Shrine's gate.

F.n: Kizakura Kappa Country (黄桜 カッパカントリー)
F.w: Brewery restaurant of Kizakura, one of Fushimi's big houses — the one place to drink both its sake and its own craft beer.

F.ad: Former Gekkeikan headquarters, Fushimi Sake District, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto
F.w: The district's visitor café: sample sets from several Fushimi breweries in the old Gekkeikan HQ building.

F.ad: In front of Nanzen-ji's Sanmon gate, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto
F.w: The classic Nanzen-ji yudofu house, set in an Edo-period medical-school building and garden by the temple gate.

F.ad: Beside Nanzen-ji, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (garden of Chōshō-in)
F.w: Has served Zen-temple tofu for centuries in a garden just outside Nanzen-ji — the most atmospheric yudofu in town.

F.n: Yudōfu Sagano (湯豆腐 嵯峨野)
F.w: Arashiyama's spacious, reliable yudofu house — the easy sit-down after the bamboo grove.
A 10-seat downtown counter whose 100% seafood broth is the anti-kotteri Kyoto bowl; Leaf KYOTO reports nine straight years of Michelin Bib Gourmand.
One MICHELIN Star yakitori counter; the name means 'the future of yakitori'.

F.ad: B1F The Ritz-Carlton Kyoto, Nakagyō-ku, Kyoto
F.w: One MICHELIN Star tempura counter by the Kamo River, in the Ritz-Carlton.
MICHELIN-selected yakitori counter downtown.
A tiny, cult sake bar (a soba shop by day) whose owner's by-the-glass list is a crash course in nihonshu.
Kyoto's 'temple to quality drinks' — a vast sake and malt-whisky library behind a polished counter.
Nordic-cool cocktail bar inside a converted Gion okiya.
A magician's cocktail den — floating couch, smoking elixirs — profiled by The Japan Times.
Asia's 50 Best Bars (No. 81, 2023 51–100 list): a wood-panelled backstreet bar of under 30 seats.

F.n: Gyoza Hohei (ぎょうざ 歩兵)
F.w: Gion's beloved gyoza counter (a past Bib Gourmand, 2017 on) — Kyoto's answer to the after-hours dumpling.

F.ad: Shijō Sakai-machi, Nakagyō-ku, Kyoto (steps from Nishiki Market)
F.w: The downtown eel specialist by Nishiki: crisp-skinned Kansai-style grilled unagi.
A signboardless tachi-gui soba bar on Kiyamachi; soba from its own upstairs noodle workshop, open till 23:00.

F.n: Grill Hasegawa (グリル はせがわ)
F.ad: 68 Oyama (Koyama) Shimo-Uchigawara-chō, Kita-ku, Kyoto (5 min from Kitaōji Stn)
F.w: Kitaōji's long-queued yōshoku institution — the definitive Kyoto hamburg steak.
Nishiki's dashimaki specialist: watch the omelettes being rolled in copper pans.
A Nishiki fishmonger-grill since 1919 — grilled-fish skewers to eat walking the arcade.
Home of Nishiki's most photographed snack, the candied baby octopus with a quail-egg head.
The Kyoto-tofu maker's Nishiki stand — the soy-milk mini-doughnut queue is a market ritual.

F.n: Itohkyuemon Uji Honten (伊藤久右衛門 宇治本店)
F.w: Uji tea house founded in 1832; its main-store café is a matcha-parfait pilgrimage.

F.ad: Uji, Kyoto (main store, in a 100-year-old building)
F.w: Tea merchant since 1860 whose Uji main store serves matcha desserts in a century-old building.
Nara's famous high-speed mochitsuki show; the mugwort mochi is eaten warm off the board.

F.n: Shizuka Nara Park (志津香 公園店)
F.w: Nara's best-known kamameshi house; long lunchtime queues by Nara Park.

F.ad: Beside Togetsukyō Bridge, Saga, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto
F.w: Soba in an old mansion overlooking the Katsura River and Togetsukyō — the classic Arashiyama lunch.
Kyoto's flagship craft brewery, founded by an American, a Welshman and a Canadian; weekend tasting room at the brewery.

F.ad: Opposite Katsura Imperial Villa, Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto
F.w: Long-established wagashi house facing Katsura Rikyū; red-bean paste still cooked the original way in a wood-fired okudo-san.

F.ad: Near Fushimi Inari Taisha, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto
F.w: The fox shrine's kitsune-udon stop: noodles made by hand each morning, tofu from a favourite Kyoto maker.

F.ad: Below Fushimi Inari Taisha, near JR Inari Stn, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto
F.w: Specialty-coffee stop at the foot of the torii tunnels — the pre-hike espresso.

F.ad: Within the Daitoku-ji temple complex, Murasakino, Kita-ku, Kyoto
F.w: Shōjin lunches in a sub-temple garden of Daitoku-ji, served since 1963.

F.n: Omen Ginkakuji Honten (名代おめん 銀閣寺本店)
F.ad: Below Ginkaku-ji (3 min from Ginkakuji-mae bus stop), Sakyō-ku, Kyoto
F.w: Since 1967 the Philosopher's-Path udon stop: thick noodles dipped in hot broth with a tray of condiments.
Since 1899 the queue-worthy mame-mochi shop at the old Ōhara road entrance to the city.

F.n: Bunnosuke Chaya Kyoto Honten (京甘味 文の助茶屋 京都本店)
F.w: A sweet house founded in 1909; the classic warabi-mochi stop on the Kiyomizu approach.

F.n: Sōhonke Yudofu Okutan Kiyomizu (総本家ゆどうふ 奥丹清水)
F.w: The Kiyomizu branch of the centuries-old Okutan tofu house, in a garden off Ninenzaka.

F.n: Starbucks Coffee Kyoto Ninenzaka Yasaka Chaya
F.w: The machiya Starbucks on the Kiyomizu approach — a traditional-house interior and a viral photo stop.

F.n: Kyoto Ramen Koji (京都拉麺小路)
F.w: Kyoto Station's ramen street — eight branches of famous regional shops on the 10th floor.
Kibune's laid-back riverside inn: catch sōmen from running water on a platform over the stream (Jun–Sep).

F.ad: Ine Bay (by the funaya), Ine-chō, Yosa-gun, Kyoto Prefecture
F.w: Founded 1754 — 'the sake brewery closest to the sea in Japan', facing the Ine funaya boathouses.
